hypotheses.title: DistributionCreator hasSigned bypass via tx.origin
hypotheses.description: The `hasSigned` modifier checks `userSignatureWhitelist[tx.origin] == 0` and `userSignatures[tx.origin] != messageHash`. This means if the `tx.origin` (the EOA that initiated the transaction) has signed the conditions or is whitelisted, any contract called by that EOA can create campaigns without the contract itself having signed. An attacker can deploy a malicious contract that calls `createCampaign` on behalf of any user who has signed the conditions, bypassing the signature requirement for the attacker's own campaigns.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Victim (any user who has called `acceptConditions()`) interacts with a malicious contract. 2. The malicious contract calls `DistributionCreator.createCampaign()` with attacker-controlled parameters. 3. The `hasSigned` modifier checks `tx.origin` (the victim) and passes because the victim has signed. 4. The campaign is created, and the attacker can set `newCampaign.creator = address(0)` so the creator defaults to `msg.sender` (the malicious contract) or set it to any address. 5. The attacker can create campaigns without ever signing the terms, using the victim's signature.
hypotheses.impact: Any user who has signed the terms can be used as a proxy to create campaigns without signing, bypassing the terms acceptance requirement. This undermines the legal/terms enforcement and allows unauthorized campaign creation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `tx.origin` checks from the `hasSigned` modifier and only check `msg.sender`.

hypotheses.title: Distributor claim authorization bypass via tx.origin
hypotheses.description: The `_claim` function authorizes a claim if `tx.origin == user`, in addition to `msg.sender == user`. This means any contract that a user interacts with (e.g., a malicious dApp) can call `Distributor.claim()` on behalf of that user, since `tx.origin` will be the user. The attacker does not need any operator approval or signature from the user.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys a malicious contract. 2. Victim calls any function on the malicious contract (e.g., a fake "claim rewards" UI). 3. The malicious contract calls `Distributor.claim([victim], [token], [amount], [proof])`. 4. Since `tx.origin == victim`, the authorization check passes. 5. The claim is processed with the victim as the user, and the recipient defaults to the victim (or can be overridden if `msg.sender != user` is false — here `msg.sender` is the malicious contract, so recipient defaults to user). However, the attacker can also pass a custom recipient via `claimWithRecipient` since `msg.sender != user` is true, so the recipient override logic applies: `if (msg.sender != user || recipient == address(0))` — since `msg.sender != user`, the code uses the user-set recipient or defaults to user. Wait — the attacker cannot set an arbitrary recipient because the condition `msg.sender != user` is true, so it falls into the branch that uses `claimRecipient[user][token]` or defaults to user. So the attacker cannot redirect funds. But the attacker can force the victim to claim at an inopportune time, or more importantly, the attacker can claim on behalf of the victim and the victim's `claimed` state is updated. This is a griefing/forced-claim issue, not direct theft. However, if the victim has set a `claimRecipient` to an attacker-controlled address (unlikely), or if the attacker can front-run a legitimate claim... Actually the real issue: the attacker can call `claim` with `tx.origin == user` and `msg.sender == attacker_contract`. The recipient logic: `if (msg.sender != user || recipient == address(0))` — since `msg.sender != user`, it uses `claimRecipient[user][token]` or defaults to user. So funds go to user or user's set recipient. Not direct theft. But the attacker can cause the victim to claim when the victim didn't want to, potentially triggering tax events or locking funds in vesting contracts. More critically, if the victim is a contract that has a `claimRecipient` set to itself and a callback... Actually, the more serious issue is that `tx.origin` authorization allows any contract to act as the user, which breaks the intended authorization model. If the user has set a `claimRecipient` to a contract that has a vulnerable `onClaim` callback, the attacker can trigger it. But the callback is only called if `data.length != 0`, and the attacker controls `data`. So the attacker can call `claimWithRecipient` with `tx.origin == user`, `msg.sender == attacker`, and pass arbitrary `data` to trigger the `onClaim` callback on the recipient (which defaults to user or user's set recipient). If the user is a contract with an `onClaim` function that has side effects, the attacker can trigger it. This is a significant authorization bypass.
hypotheses.impact: Any external actor can force a user to claim rewards by calling through a contract the user interacts with, potentially triggering unintended callbacks, tax events, or state changes in the user's contract. In the worst case, if the user is a contract with a vulnerable `onClaim` callback, the attacker can exploit it.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `tx.origin != user` check and only allow `msg.sender == user` or explicit operator authorization.

hypotheses.title: Anyone can call setFeeRecipient to overwrite wrapper fee recipient
hypotheses.description: `setFeeRecipient()` is declared `external` with no access modifier, unlike the internal `_setFeeRecipient()`. Any untrusted caller can invoke it to re-read `DistributionCreator.feeRecipient()` and overwrite the wrapper's `feeRecipient` state variable. While the value is sourced from the trusted creator, the function is still a privileged setter reachable by anyone and can be used to force state changes at arbitrary times (e.g., front-running a governance change to the creator's feeRecipient).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker calls `NativeTokenWrapper.setFeeRecipient()` directly. 2. The wrapper re-reads `DistributionCreator(distributionCreator).feeRecipient()` and writes it to storage. 3. If governance has just changed the creator's feeRecipient, the attacker can force the wrapper to adopt the new value before intended, or repeatedly trigger state writes.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized state mutation of a privileged setter; potential desynchronization between wrapper and governance intent; event spam.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyMinterOrGovernor` (or `onlyGovernor`) to `setFeeRecipient()`.

hypotheses.title: Anyone can call setFeeRecipient on PufferPointTokenWrapper
hypotheses.description: `setFeeRecipient()` is `external` with no modifier, exposing a privileged setter to any caller. It calls `_setFeeRecipient()` which reads `DistributionCreator(distributionCreator).feeRecipient()` and writes it to storage. An untrusted actor can invoke this at will, forcing the wrapper to adopt the current creator feeRecipient and emitting `FeeRecipientUpdated` events.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker calls `PufferPointTokenWrapper.setFeeRecipient()`. 2. Wrapper reads creator's feeRecipient and stores it. 3. Attacker can repeat to spam events or force sync at attacker-chosen times.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized privileged state change; potential desync with governance-controlled feeRecipient; event spam.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `setFeeRecipient()` with `onlyGovernor` or `onlyGuardian`.

hypotheses.title: Distributor._claim allows tx.origin to claim on behalf of any user
hypotheses.description: The authorization check accepts `tx.origin == user` as sufficient to claim for `user`. Any contract that a user interacts with (e.g. a malicious dApp, a phishing contract, or a compromised router) can call `Distributor.claim` with `users[i] = victim` and valid Merkle proofs (which are public), and the check passes because `tx.origin` is the victim. The tokens are then sent to the attacker-controlled `recipient` (since `msg.sender != user`, the recipient defaults to `claimRecipient[user][token]` or `user`, but the attacker can also pre-set nothing and instead route via a contract that the victim calls — more directly, the attacker can pass `recipients[i]` only if `msg.sender == user`, so the practical exploit is that the attacker's contract calls claim and the tokens go to the victim, but the attacker can front-run/force claims and manipulate `claimed` state, or use `claimRecipient` set by the victim to a contract the attacker controls).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim has unclaimed Merkl rewards. 2) Attacker deploys a contract that calls `Distributor.claim([victim], [token], [amount], [proof])`. 3) `tx.origin == victim` because the victim is induced to call the attacker's contract (e.g. via a phishing site or a malicious dApp). 4) The check passes; the claim executes. 5) If the victim previously set a `claimRecipient` to an attacker-influenced address, funds are redirected; otherwise the attacker can at least force-claim and manipulate `claimed` state / timing.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized claims on behalf of users; potential redirection of rewards if a custom recipient is set; griefing of claim timing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `tx.origin == user` branch; require `msg.sender == user` or an explicit operator authorization.

hypotheses.title: PufferPointTokenWrapper::claimable uses hardcoded timestamp gating
hypotheses.description: `_claimable` requires `block.timestamp > 1740816009` (a hardcoded future date) in addition to per-vesting `unlockTimestamp`. This is an implicit global cliff that cannot be changed by governance. Any user whose vesting timestamps have all passed still cannot claim until this hardcoded time, and no admin function exists to adjust it, creating a permanent behavioral lockout if the intended semantics change.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A — this is not exploitable by an untrusted actor but is a hardcoded constant that locks user funds until a fixed calendar date.
hypotheses.impact: Funds frozen for users until the hardcoded timestamp, with no way to adapt to schedule changes.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace the hardcoded literal with a configurable state variable controllable by governance, and revert if unchanged when unused.

hypotheses.title: Dispute period can be frozen indefinitely by disputer via repeated disputes
hypotheses.description: `disputeTree` sets `disputer = msg.sender` and blocks `updateTree` while a dispute is active. The only way to clear `disputer` is `resolveDispute`, which is governor-only. A whitelisted disputer (or anyone who can call `Disputer.toggleDispute`) can repeatedly open disputes; each time the governor resolves one, the disputer can immediately open another as long as `block.timestamp < endOfDisputePeriod`. Because `resolveDispute(false)` extends `endOfDisputePeriod` to a fresh epoch window, the disputer can keep the tree frozen indefinitely, blocking all tree updates and forcing claims to use the stale `lastTree.merkleRoot`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker (whitelisted in `Disputer`) calls `toggleDispute` right before `endOfDisputePeriod`. 2. Governor resolves with `valid=false`, which resets `endOfDisputePeriod` to a new future epoch. 3. Attacker calls `toggleDispute` again immediately (still within the new window). 4. Repeat — `disputer` is never zero long enough for `updateTree` to succeed, and `getMerkleRoot()` keeps returning `lastTree.merkleRoot`.
hypotheses.impact: Merkle tree updates are permanently blocked; new reward epochs cannot be published; users can only claim against the stale root, so newly earned rewards are unreachable. Dispute deposits are also cycled, but the primary damage is frozen reward distribution.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a cooldown after a dispute is resolved (e.g., require `block.timestamp > endOfDisputePeriod + cooldown` before a new dispute), or cap the number of consecutive disputes per address, or require the disputer to be a governor-appointed role.

hypotheses.title: DistributionCreator.hasSigned trusts tx.origin, enabling signature bypass via phishing contract
hypotheses.description: The `hasSigned` modifier accepts `userSignatureWhitelist[tx.origin] != 0` or `userSignatures[tx.origin] == messageHash` as valid authorization. A malicious contract called by a whitelisted or signed user can therefore create campaigns on that user's behalf without the user's per-call consent. Combined with `_computeFees` applying `feeRebate[msg.sender]` (the malicious contract, not the user), the attacker can also manipulate fee accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim `V` has previously called `acceptConditions()` (or is whitelisted). 2) Attacker deploys `M` and lures `V` into calling `M.f()`. 3) `M` calls `DistributionCreator.createCampaign(params)` with `params.creator = V` and `params.rewardToken` a token `V` has approved to the creator. 4) `hasSigned` passes because `tx.origin == V`. 5) `_pullTokens` pulls from `msg.sender` (M) if `creatorBalance[V]` is insufficient — but if `V` has a predeposited balance, it is drained. 6) Fees are computed against `feeRebate[M]`, not `V`.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized campaign creation using victim's predeposited balance; fee rebate manipulation; griefing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove `tx.origin` from the `hasSigned` check; require `msg.sender` to be signed/whitelisted.

hypotheses.title: Distributor._claim transfers tokens before callback, enabling cross-function reentrancy
hypotheses.description: In `_claim`, the state update `claimed[user][token] = Claim(...)` happens before the token transfer, but the `nonReentrant` guard only protects `_claim` itself. The `IClaimRecipient(recipient).onClaim(...)` callback is invoked after `safeTransfer`, and although the callback is wrapped in try/catch, the recipient contract can reenter other non-guarded functions such as `toggleOperator`, `setClaimRecipient`, or `toggleMainOperatorStatus` during the callback. More importantly, the callback executes after the transfer but the `nonReentrant` modifier is on `_claim`, so reentering `claim` is blocked — however reentering `disputeTree` or `updateTree` is not blocked by the same guard, and `disputeTree` reads `endOfDisputePeriod` and `disputer` which can be manipulated mid-claim.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys a malicious recipient contract and sets it as `claimRecipient` for themselves. 2. Attacker calls `claim` with a valid proof; `_claim` transfers tokens to the malicious recipient. 3. The malicious recipient's `onClaim` callback reenters `disputeTree` (which is not `nonReentrant`) or `toggleOperator` to alter state while the outer claim is still executing. 4. Because `disputeTree` only checks `disputer == address(0)` and `block.timestamp < endOfDisputePeriod`, the attacker can freeze the tree mid-claim.
hypotheses.impact: An attacker can manipulate dispute state or operator permissions during a claim, potentially freezing the Merkle tree or altering claim authorization mid-transaction, leading to incorrect accounting or denial of service for other claimants.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply `nonReentrant` to all state-mutating external functions that interact with claim state (`disputeTree`, `toggleOperator`, `setClaimRecipient`, `toggleMainOperatorStatus`), or move the callback invocation before the state update and transfer.

hypotheses.title: NativeTokenWrapper._beforeTokenTransfer reverts on any ETH transfer failure, bricking claims
hypotheses.description: When the distributor transfers wrapper tokens to a user, `_beforeTokenTransfer` performs `to.call{value: amount}("")` and reverts with `WithdrawalFailed` if the call fails. A user whose address is a contract that rejects ETH (or a contract with a reverting `receive`/`fallback`) can never receive their claim, and because the distributor's `_claim` loop processes all entries in one transaction, a single such recipient reverts the entire batch, blocking claims for all other users in the same call.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys a contract that reverts on receiving ETH and gets it whitelisted as a campaign recipient (or simply is a legitimate user whose wallet is a contract). 2. Attacker (or any user) calls `Distributor.claim` with an array that includes the attacker's address. 3. `_beforeTokenTransfer` reverts, reverting the whole `claim` transaction. 4. Attacker can also be included in other users' batched claims to grief them.
hypotheses.impact: Claims for the affected user are permanently stuck (funds locked in the wrapper/distributor), and any batched claim including that user reverts, enabling griefing of other users' claims.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a pull-based pattern (credit the recipient and let them withdraw) or wrap the ETH send in a try/catch and skip/queue failed transfers instead of reverting the whole claim.

hypotheses.title: DistributionCreator campaign ID collision due to missing nonce
hypotheses.description: The `campaignId` function computes the ID as `keccak256(abi.encodePacked(CHAIN_ID, creator, rewardToken, campaignType, startTimestamp, duration, campaignData))`. There is no nonce or unique identifier. If a creator creates two campaigns with the same parameters (same reward token, type, start timestamp, duration, and campaign data), the second creation will revert with `CampaignAlreadyExists`. This is intentional for preventing duplicates, but it means a creator cannot create two identical campaigns. More importantly, if a campaign is created and then the creator wants to create another identical campaign later (e.g., after the first one ends), they cannot because the ID is the same. This is a design limitation, not a security vulnerability per se. However, an attacker could front-run a creator's `createCampaign` transaction with the same parameters, causing the creator's transaction to revert. The attacker would need to pay the fees and create the campaign themselves, but they could set `creator` to the victim's address (since `newCampaign.creator` can be set to any address). Wait — the attacker can set `newCampaign.creator = victim` and create the campaign, paying the fees from their own balance (since `_pullTokens` uses `msg.sender` for the transfer if the creator's balance is insufficient). The attacker would be paying for the campaign but the creator would be the victim. This is a griefing attack.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker sees a pending `createCampaign` transaction from victim in the mempool. 2. Attacker front-runs with the same parameters but sets `creator = victim`. 3. The attacker's transaction succeeds, creating the campaign with the victim as creator. 4. The victim's transaction reverts with `CampaignAlreadyExists`. 5. The attacker has paid the fees but the campaign is created with the victim as creator. The victim cannot create the campaign again.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing attack: the victim's transaction reverts, and the attacker can create campaigns with the victim as creator, potentially causing confusion or unwanted campaigns.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include a nonce or a unique identifier (e.g., `block.timestamp` or a user-provided salt) in the campaign ID computation.

hypotheses.title: Disputer.toggleDispute lets anyone drain whitelisted disputer's pre-funded balance
hypotheses.description: `toggleDispute` is callable by any whitelisted address. If the Disputer contract already holds `disputeAmount` (e.g. from a prior deposit or leftover funds), the caller does not need to supply any tokens, yet `distributor.disputeTree(reason)` is invoked and the contract's balance is consumed as the dispute deposit. A whitelisted actor can therefore repeatedly trigger disputes using other users' pre-funded tokens, and if the dispute is resolved as invalid, the deposit is sent to the governor (not back to the original funder), permanently losing those funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A whitelisted disputer pre-funds the Disputer contract (or a prior dispute left residual balance). 2) Attacker (also whitelisted) calls `toggleDispute("x")` with zero balance of their own. 3) `contractBalance >= disputeAmount` so no transferFrom occurs; `disputeTree` pulls `disputeAmount` from the Disputer. 4) Governor resolves as invalid → deposit is sent to governor; the original funder's tokens are gone. 5) Repeat to grief.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of pre-funded dispute collateral belonging to other whitelisted users; griefing of the dispute mechanism.
hypotheses.recommendation: Always pull `disputeAmount` from `msg.sender` (or track per-user deposits) rather than relying on the contract's pooled balance.

hypotheses.title: Disputer.toggleDispute pulls only shortfall, leaving distributor to pull full amount
hypotheses.description: `toggleDispute` computes `contractBalance` and only transfers `disputeAmount - contractBalance` from `msg.sender` when the contract is short. But `Distributor.disputeTree` then does `safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), disputeAmount)` where `msg.sender` is the Disputer contract. The Disputer only holds `disputeAmount` after the top-up, so the transfer succeeds only if the Disputer's balance exactly equals `disputeAmount`. If the Disputer already holds more than `disputeAmount` (e.g., leftover from a prior dispute that was resolved valid and returned, or a prior failed attempt), the shortfall logic is skipped and the full `disputeAmount` is pulled from the Disputer's balance — but the Disputer never refunds the excess to the caller, and the caller's `transferFrom` is skipped entirely. Conversely, if the Disputer holds exactly `disputeAmount` from a previous caller's top-up, a second caller can dispute for free using the first caller's funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (whitelisted) calls `toggleDispute` when Disputer balance is 0; attacker pays `disputeAmount`. 2) Dispute is resolved invalid by governor; `disputeAmount` is sent to governor, not back to Disputer — so this path drains. 3) Alternatively, if a prior dispute was resolved valid, `disputeAmount` is returned to the Disputer (the disputer), leaving the Disputer holding `disputeAmount`. 4) A second whitelisted attacker calls `toggleDispute`; `contractBalance >= disputeAmount`, so no `transferFrom` from attacker occurs; `distributor.disputeTree` pulls `disputeAmount` from the Disputer. Attacker disputes for free with the first disputer's returned collateral.
hypotheses.impact: Free disputes funded by other users' collateral; loss of funds for the original disputer whose returned deposit is consumed by another party.
hypotheses.recommendation: Always pull `disputeAmount` from `msg.sender` in `toggleDispute` (or refund any excess Disputer balance to the caller), and have the Disputer approve only the exact amount needed per call.

hypotheses.title: NativeTokenWrapper._beforeTokenTransfer sends ETH before state update, reentrancy via receive
hypotheses.description: `_beforeTokenTransfer` performs `to.call{value: amount}("")` before the ERC20 transfer state is finalized. If `to` is a contract with a malicious `receive`/`fallback`, it can reenter the wrapper's `mint`, `mintWithNative`, `toggleAllowance`, or `setMinter` functions. Since `_beforeTokenTransfer` is called during `_transfer` from the distributor, the attacker can reenter and mint additional wrapper tokens or alter `isAllowed` mappings before the outer transfer completes.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys a contract that, on receiving ETH, calls `NativeTokenWrapper.mintWithNative()` or `mint()` (if they are the minter) or `toggleAllowance`. 2. Attacker triggers a claim from the Distributor that transfers wrapper tokens to their contract. 3. During `_beforeTokenTransfer`, the ETH call invokes the attacker's `receive`, which reenters the wrapper. 4. The attacker mints extra tokens or toggles allowances, then the outer transfer completes with inconsistent state.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can mint unbacked wrapper tokens or manipulate `isAllowed` to bypass burn-on-transfer restrictions, leading to inflated balances and potential drainage of underlying ETH.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a reentrancy guard on the wrapper's transfer path, or perform the ETH transfer after all state updates (e.g., in `_afterTokenTransfer`).

hypotheses.title: _computeFees rounds in favor of the creator, not the protocol
hypotheses.description: `distributionAmountMinusFees = (distributionAmount * (BASE_9 - _fees)) / BASE_9` truncates downward, so the creator keeps the rounding remainder and the protocol receives slightly less than the nominal fee. For small `distributionAmount` relative to `BASE_9`, the fee can round to zero entirely, letting a creator avoid fees by splitting a campaign into many tiny campaigns (each above the token minimum but small enough that the fee truncates to 0).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker picks a reward token with a low `rewardTokenMinAmounts`. 2. Attacker creates many campaigns each with `amount` just above the minimum such that `(amount * _fees) / BASE_9 == 0`. 3. Each campaign pays zero protocol fee while still being valid.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol fee revenue is systematically under-collected; fee evasion via campaign splitting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Round fees up (e.g., `(distributionAmount * _fees + BASE_9 - 1) / BASE_9`) or enforce a minimum fee per campaign.

hypotheses.title: NativeTokenWrapper._beforeTokenTransfer sends ETH on every transfer from distributor
hypotheses.description: `_beforeTokenTransfer` sends `amount` ETH to `to` whenever `from == distributor || to == feeRecipient`. But `_afterTokenTransfer` burns tokens sent to non-allowed addresses. If a claim transfers wrapper tokens from the distributor to a user, ETH is sent to the user, but the wrapper tokens are then burned. The contract's ETH balance must cover all outstanding wrapper tokens; if the minter mints wrapper tokens without depositing matching ETH (via `mint` rather than `mintWithNative`), the contract becomes insolvent and later claims revert.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Minter (trusted) mints wrapper tokens via `mint` without ETH. 2. Users claim; `_beforeTokenTransfer` tries to send ETH but contract has insufficient balance. 3. Claims revert, freezing user rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Insolvency of the wrapper; frozen claims.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `mint` to be backed by ETH (e.g., only allow `mintWithNative`), or track ETH backing per minted token.

hypotheses.title: DistributionCreator::createCampaigns does not check startTimestamp is in the future
hypotheses.description: `_createCampaign` validates duration and reward token whitelist but never validates `startTimestamp`. Because `campaignId` includes `startTimestamp`, a caller can create campaigns with `startTimestamp = 0` (or any past value), encoding a "campaign" that already started at the epoch of 0. The Merkl engine may reject these but the fee is still pulled, and `reallocateCampaignRewards` uses `startTimestamp + duration` for the reallocation gate — a past start would allow immediate reallocation by an operator even before the intended schedule.
hypotheses.attackPath: An operator A of creator C calls `createCampaign` with `startTimestamp = 0` and small duration. `_createCampaign` accepts (duration >= HOUR). Fee is deducted from A/C. Because `startTimestamp + duration <= block.timestamp` immediately, A can call `reallocateCampaignRewards` right away, diverting any claimed-but-unclaimed rewards before any distribution occurs.
hypotheses.impact: Premature reallocation of campaign rewards, corrupting reward accounting; fees paid for typically invalid campaigns.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `newCampaign.startTimestamp >= block.timestamp` in `_createCampaign`.

hypotheses.title: PullTokenWrapperWithdraw._beforeTokenTransfer external Aave withdraw before state finalization
hypotheses.description: `_beforeTokenTransfer` calls `IAavePool(pool).withdraw(underlying, amount, to)` which sends underlying tokens to `to` before the ERC20 transfer state is finalized. If `to` is a malicious contract, it can reenter the wrapper's `mint`, `setHolder`, or `setFeeRecipient` functions. The Aave pool itself may also invoke callbacks on `to` if it's a contract, enabling reentrancy into the wrapper or the Distributor's claim flow.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys a malicious contract as the claim recipient. 2. Attacker triggers a claim that transfers wrapper tokens to their contract. 3. During `_beforeTokenTransfer`, Aave's `withdraw` sends underlying tokens to the attacker's contract, which reenters `PullTokenWrapperWithdraw.mint()` (if holder) or `setHolder` to manipulate state. 4. The attacker can mint wrapper tokens or change the holder to drain funds.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can mint unbacked wrapper tokens or redirect the holder to drain underlying Aave positions, causing loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to the wrapper's transfer functions and ensure all state updates occur before external calls.

hypotheses.title: ReferralRegistry.becomeReferrer sends ETH to program.owner before state update
hypotheses.description: In `becomeReferrer`, when `program.cost > 0` and `paymentToken == address(0)`, the contract sends ETH to `program.owner` via `call{value: msg.value}` before updating `refererStatus`, `referrerCodeMapping`, and `codeToReferrer`. If `program.owner` is a malicious contract, it can reenter `becomeReferrer` with the same `referrerCode` before the state is updated, bypassing the `codeToReferrer[key][referrerCode] != address(0)` check.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker creates a referral program with a malicious `owner` contract. 2. Attacker calls `becomeReferrer` with a `referrerCode`. 3. The ETH transfer to `program.owner` triggers the malicious contract's `receive`, which reenters `becomeReferrer` with the same `referrerCode`. 4. The check `codeToReferrer[key][referrerCode] != address(0)` still passes because state hasn't been updated, allowing the attacker to register the same code multiple times or bypass authorization.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can register duplicate referrer codes, bypass `requiresAuthorization` checks, or drain ETH by reentering with the same payment.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update all state (`refererStatus`, `referrerCodeMapping`, `codeToReferrer`) before sending ETH, or use a reentrancy guard.

hypotheses.title: PullTokenWrapperAllow/Withdraw/TransferV0 pull from holder without allowance check, bricking claims
hypotheses.description: `_beforeTokenTransfer` calls `IERC20(token).safeTransferFrom(holder, to, amount)` during claims. If the holder has not granted (or has revoked) sufficient allowance to the wrapper, the transfer reverts, and because `Distributor._claim` iterates over all entries in one transaction, a single failing wrapper claim reverts the entire batch. The holder is a trusted role, but the failure mode is triggered by the holder's allowance state, which can be changed at any time and is not validated at claim time.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Holder revokes allowance (or allowance is exhausted). 2. Any user calls `Distributor.claim` for a token whose wrapper is this contract. 3. `safeTransferFrom` reverts, reverting the whole claim transaction. 4. Users cannot claim their rewards until the holder restores allowance; if the holder is unresponsive, funds are stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Reward claims for the affected wrapper token are frozen; batched claims including that token revert for all users in the batch.
hypotheses.recommendation: Check allowance before transfer and skip/queue the claim if insufficient, or use a pull-based withdrawal so a single failing token does not revert the whole batch.

hypotheses.title: ReferralRegistry.acknowledgeReferrer unbounded loop over referred list can be griefed
hypotheses.description: When a user changes referrer, `acknowledgeReferrer` iterates over `keyToReferred[key][previousReferrer]` to remove the user. An attacker can become a referrer (if the program allows it) and then have many addresses acknowledge them, growing the array. When a victim who previously acknowledged the attacker tries to switch referrers, the loop over the large array can exceed the block gas limit and revert, permanently preventing the victim from changing referrers.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker becomes a referrer for a key (via `becomeReferrer` or `allowReferrer`). 2. Attacker uses many addresses to call `acknowledgeReferrer(key, attacker)`, growing `keyToReferred[key][attacker]`. 3. Victim (who previously acknowledged attacker) calls `acknowledgeReferrer` to switch to a new referrer. 4. The loop over the large array reverts on gas, locking the victim into the attacker's referral.
hypotheses.impact: Victim cannot change referrers; referral accounting is frozen for that user, and any downstream reward attribution based on the referrer is stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace the linear scan with a mapping-based index (e.g., store each referred user's index in the array) so removal is O(1).

hypotheses.title: NativeTokenWrapper _beforeTokenTransfer sends ETH to feeRecipient without checking
hypotheses.description: The `_beforeTokenTransfer` function sends ETH to the `to` address when `from == distributor || to == feeRecipient`. This is done via a low-level `call` with all available gas. If the `to` address is a malicious contract, it can reenter the `NativeTokenWrapper` or the `Distributor` during the ETH transfer. The `Distributor` has a `nonReentrant` modifier on `_claim`, but the `NativeTokenWrapper` does not have reentrancy protection. An attacker could exploit this to manipulate the wrapper's state or drain funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker creates a malicious contract that implements a `receive()` function that reenters `NativeTokenWrapper` or `Distributor`. 2. Attacker triggers a claim that sends ETH to the malicious contract (e.g., by setting the malicious contract as the recipient). 3. During the ETH transfer, the malicious contract's `receive()` is called. 4. The malicious contract reenters `NativeTokenWrapper` (e.g., calls `mintWithNative` or `transfer`) or `Distributor` (e.g., calls `claim` again). 5. Since `NativeTokenWrapper` has no reentrancy guard, the attacker can manipulate balances or drain funds.
hypotheses.impact: Potential reentrancy attack leading to loss of funds or incorrect accounting in the `NativeTokenWrapper`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to `NativeTokenWrapper` or use `transfer` instead of `call` (though `transfer` is not recommended due to gas limits). Alternatively, follow the checks-effects-interactions pattern.

hypotheses.title: PullTokenWrapperAllow and PullTokenWrapperTransfer lack reentrancy protection
hypotheses.description: The `_beforeTokenTransfer` function in `PullTokenWrapperAllow` calls `IERC20(token).safeTransferFrom(holder, to, amount)`. If the `token` is a malicious ERC20 with a callback (e.g., ERC777), the `to` address can reenter the wrapper during the transfer. The wrapper has no reentrancy guard. Similarly, `PullTokenWrapperTransfer` calls `IERC20(token).safeTransfer(to, amount)` in `_beforeTokenTransfer`, which can also trigger a callback. An attacker could exploit this to manipulate the wrapper's state or drain funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys a malicious ERC20 token with a callback in `transferFrom` or `transfer`. 2. Attacker sets up a campaign with this token as the reward token. 3. When a user claims, the `_beforeTokenTransfer` is triggered, calling the malicious token's `transferFrom` or `transfer`. 4. The malicious token's callback reenters the wrapper (e.g., calls `mint` or `transfer`). 5. Since there is no reentrancy guard, the attacker can manipulate balances or drain funds.
hypotheses.impact: Potential reentrancy attack leading to loss of funds or incorrect accounting in the wrapper.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to the wrapper contracts or ensure that the token transfers are done in a way that prevents reentrancy (e.g., using a pull pattern).

hypotheses.title: Distributor._claim lets mainOperators[operator][address(0)] claim any token for any user
hypotheses.description: The authorization check treats `mainOperators[msg.sender][address(0)] != 0` as sufficient to claim any token for any user. A governor can grant this via `toggleMainOperatorStatus(operator, address(0))`. Once granted, the operator can claim all tokens for all users. Combined with the fact that `claimWithRecipient` allows the caller to specify arbitrary `recipients` when `msg.sender != user` only if `recipient == address(0)` (otherwise the user-set recipient is used), the operator can still force claims and, if the user has set a `claimRecipient` to an address the operator controls, redirect funds. More critically, the operator can claim on behalf of users who have not authorized them, draining the distributor's token balances to the users (or to user-set recipients), which can be used to grief or to front-run legitimate claims.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A main operator is authorized for `address(0)` (all tokens). 2) Operator calls `claim([victim], [token], [amount], [proof])` for any victim. 3) The check passes via `mainOperators[msg.sender][address(0)] != 0`. 4) Tokens are sent to the victim (or victim's `claimRecipient`). 5) If the victim's `claimRecipient` is a contract the operator can influence, funds are redirected.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized claims on behalf of arbitrary users; potential redirection of rewards; griefing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `mainOperators[operator][address(0)]` to only claim for users who have explicitly opted in, or remove the wildcard token authorization.

hypotheses.title: DistributionCreator._computeFees applies rebate to msg.sender, not creator, enabling fee evasion via operator
hypotheses.description: `_computeFees` applies `feeRebate[msg.sender]` rather than `feeRebate[creator]`. A creator with a high fee rebate can authorize an operator (via `toggleCampaignOperator`) who has no rebate, or conversely, an operator with a high rebate can create campaigns on behalf of a creator with no rebate, paying reduced fees. More directly, a creator can set up a fresh address with a high rebate (if governance grants it) and use it as `msg.sender` while the campaign's `creator` is a different address, effectively laundering the rebate. Since `_pullTokens` pulls from `creator`'s balance or `msg.sender`, the fee is computed on `msg.sender`'s rebate but the funds come from `creator`, creating a mismatch.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Governance grants a high `feeRebate` to address A. 2) Address A calls `createCampaign` with `newCampaign.creator = B` (a different address with no rebate). 3) `_computeFees` uses `feeRebate[A]` (high), so fees are low. 4) `_pullTokens` pulls from B's balance or A's balance. 5) B's campaign is created with reduced fees, bypassing the intended fee structure.
hypotheses.impact: Fee evasion; protocol loses fee revenue.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply the fee rebate based on `creator`, not `msg.sender`, or require `msg.sender == creator` for rebate eligibility.

hypotheses.title: PullTokenWrapperWithdraw withdraws full amount from Aave but only transfers `amount` to recipient
hypotheses.description: `_beforeTokenTransfer` does `IERC20(token).safeTransferFrom(holder, address(this), amount)` then `IAavePool(pool).withdraw(underlying, amount, to)`. The `withdraw` call sends `underlying` directly to `to`, but the aToken `token` transferred from `holder` to the wrapper is never returned to `holder` or burned — it accumulates in the wrapper. Over time, the wrapper holds aTokens that belong to `holder` but are not accounted for, and `holder` loses aTokens without receiving underlying. Additionally, `withdraw` may return less than `amount` if the pool has liquidity issues, but the code ignores the return value.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Any claim that triggers a transfer from `distributor` causes `_beforeTokenTransfer` to pull `amount` aTokens from `holder` and withdraw `amount` underlying to the recipient. 2) The aTokens remain in the wrapper. 3) An attacker who is `holder` (or governor) can call `recover` — but `recover` is `onlyHolderOrGovernor`, so only holder/governor can recover. However, the aTokens are effectively stuck and the holder's aToken balance is reduced without compensation.
hypotheses.impact: Holder loses aTokens; wrapper accumulates unaccounted aTokens; potential insolvency if holder's aToken balance is exhausted.
hypotheses.recommendation: After `withdraw`, transfer the withdrawn underlying to `to` and return the aTokens to `holder`, or burn the aTokens; check the return value of `withdraw`.

hypotheses.title: Disputer.toggleDispute double-pulls disputeAmount from caller
hypotheses.description: When `contractBalance < disputeAmount`, the Disputer pulls `disputeAmount - contractBalance` from `msg.sender` into itself, then calls `distributor.disputeTree(reason)`. But `Distributor.disputeTree` itself does `IERC20(disputeToken).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), disputeAmount)` — where `msg.sender` is the Disputer. So the Disputer must already hold `disputeAmount` to satisfy the distributor's pull, yet it only topped up to exactly `disputeAmount`. The leftover balance from prior disputes (or the top-up) is consumed, but the accounting is fragile: any pre-existing balance in the Disputer is silently drained by the distributor's pull, and the caller's top-up is effectively double-counted against the same dispute.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker (whitelisted) calls `toggleDispute` when Disputer holds some residual balance B < disputeAmount. 2. Attacker transfers `disputeAmount - B` to Disputer. 3. Distributor pulls `disputeAmount` from Disputer, leaving Disputer with 0. 4. If the dispute is later resolved as invalid, the deposit goes to the governor, not back to the Disputer — the attacker's funds are gone with no refund path to the Disputer.
hypotheses.impact: Whitelisted disputer's funds are permanently lost on invalid disputes; Disputer's residual balance is silently consumed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Have the Disputer transfer exactly the shortfall to the distributor and let the distributor pull from the Disputer only the amount it needs, or track per-dispute deposits explicitly.

hypotheses.title: SonicFragment.redeem uses stale supply after burn, mispricing redemptions
hypotheses.description: `redeem` computes `amountToSend = (amount * _sTokenAmount) / supply` where `supply` is the immutable total supply set at construction. However, `_burn(msg.sender, amount)` reduces the actual ERC20 total supply, but the stored `supply` variable is never updated. If `recover` is called and sets `sTokenAmount = 0`, redemptions revert. More critically, the exchange rate uses the original `supply` even after burns, so the last redeemer receives a proportionally larger share only if `sTokenAmount` is fixed — but if `sTokenAmount` is reduced by `recover`, earlier redeemers got more than their fair share, leaving later redeemers with less.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Governor calls `recover` to pull S tokens, setting `sTokenAmount = 0`. 2. All subsequent `redeem` calls revert. 3. Alternatively, if `recover` is called with a partial amount but `sTokenAmount` is zeroed, the accounting is broken.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen redemptions or unfair distribution of S tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update `supply` on burn, or use `totalSupply()` dynamically; do not zero `sTokenAmount` in `recover` without accounting for outstanding fragments.

hypotheses.title: DistributionCreator::_pullTokens misroutes funds when allowance path is used
hypotheses.description: In `_pullTokens`, when `userBalance >= campaignAmount` but `msg.sender != creator` and `senderAllowance < campaignAmount`, the function falls into a branch that transfers `campaignAmountMinusFees` from `msg.sender` to `distributor` and `fees` from `msg.sender` to `_feeRecipient`, but the creator's predeposited balance is not debited nor deducted. The intent was to spend the creator's predeposited balance — instead it uses the caller's tokens while leaving the creator's balance intact. This is not a price/oracle issue strictly, but a fund-routing accounting bug that can be exploited by an operator with a small allowance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Operator A is authorized by creator C (via `toggleCampaignOperator`) or has small allowance. 2. C has predeposited balance >= campaignAmount. 3. A calls `createCampaign` with `newCampaign.creator = C` and a large amount, giving A a small `creatorAllowance`. 4. `_pullTokens` sees `senderAllowance < campaignAmount` and pulls full amount from A, but leaves C's predeposited balance untouched. 5. A loses funds that should have come from C's balance.
hypotheses.impact: Funds are pulled from the wrong party; creator's predeposited balance remains intact though the campaign counts as created — accounting discrepancy and loss of operator funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: In the fallback branch, debit `creatorBalance[creator][rewardToken]` (or explicitly revert) instead of pulling from `msg.sender`, since predeposited balance existed.

hypotheses.title: MerklGaugeMiddlemanTemplate::notifyReward lacks slippage/min-out and uses stale params
hypotheses.description: `notifyReward` copies `gaugeParams[token][gauge]` and overwrites only `startTimestamp`, `amount`, `rewardToken`. All other fields (duration, campaignType, campaignData) are whatever the owner last set, potentially long ago. There is no minimum-reward or user-set slippage parameter supplied by `msg.sender`, so an untrusted gauge caller cannot express any bounds on the resulting campaign. If the owner's stored `params.amount` is irrelevant but `duration`/`campaignData` are stale (e.g. reference an outdated pool/wrapper), rewards can be lockable into a wrong campaign with no ability for the caller to reject.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted gauge calls `notifyReward(token, gauge, amount)`. Because there is no min-out / per-call parameter validation, the transaction proceeds using whatever character the owner has previously set. If a third party controls the gauge's `amount` (e.g. an attacker manipulating gauge accounting) they can force the campaign to be created with an unfavorable min amount check `amount * 3600 > minAmount * duration` still satisfied, locking generous rewards into a poorly-parameterized campaign with no slippage protection on the caller side.
hypotheses.impact: Rewards can be distributed under stale/misconfigured parameters (wrong duration or campaignData), with no minimal-out protection at the call site.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add explicit min-amount/min-distributed checks per call and validate `params.duration` / `params.campaignType` against expected values in `notifyReward` instead of relying on stored values only.

hypotheses.title: PufferPointTokenWrapper._afterTokenTransfer burns and creates vesting after transfer, reentrancy via underlying transfer
hypotheses.description: `_afterTokenTransfer` calls `IERC20(token()).safeTransfer(to, amount)` when `block.timestamp >= endTimestamp`, which is an external call after the burn and vesting state updates. If the underlying token has a callback (e.g., ERC-777), the recipient can reenter `claim` or `_beforeTokenTransfer` to manipulate vesting data. Additionally, `_beforeTokenTransfer` calls `safeTransferFrom` on the underlying token before minting, allowing a malicious underlying token to reenter.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker uses a malicious underlying token with a transfer hook. 2. Attacker triggers a claim from the Distributor that transfers wrapper tokens to their contract. 3. During `_afterTokenTransfer`, the underlying token's hook reenters `claim` or `_beforeTokenTransfer`. 4. The attacker can double-claim or manipulate vesting indices.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can double-claim vested tokens or corrupt vesting accounting, leading to loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to `claim` and ensure external token transfers occur after all state updates.

hypotheses.title: PufferPointTokenWrapper vesting loop can be griefed by unbounded vesting array growth
hypotheses.description: `_claimable` iterates over `userAllVestings` starting at `nextClaimIndex` and stops at the first vesting whose `unlockTimestamp` is in the future. Because `_afterTokenTransfer` pushes a new `VestingID` on every distributor→user transfer, an attacker who can cause many small transfers to a victim (e.g., by repeatedly triggering claims that route to the victim, or by being the distributor's counterparty) can grow the array. If the array grows large enough, `claim` will run out of gas and revert, permanently locking the victim's vested tokens.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker arranges for many small distributor→victim transfers (e.g., via repeated claims with tiny amounts, or by being a campaign creator whose rewards flow to the victim). 2. Each transfer pushes a new `VestingID` with a future `unlockTimestamp`. 3. Victim calls `claim`; the loop iterates over the growing array and eventually exceeds the block gas limit, reverting. 4. Victim cannot claim any vested tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Victim's vested tokens are permanently stuck because `claim` reverts on gas exhaustion; the array cannot be pruned by the victim.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap the number of vestings per user, or allow claiming in bounded batches with a user-supplied index range, or aggregate vestings with the same unlock timestamp.

hypotheses.title: Distributor._claim batch reverts if any single proof or transfer fails, blocking all claims
hypotheses.description: `_claim` processes all entries in a single loop and reverts the entire transaction if any single entry fails (invalid proof, failed token transfer, reverting callback, or a wrapper's `_beforeTokenTransfer` revert). An attacker can include a deliberately invalid entry (e.g., a bad proof or a token that reverts on transfer) in a batch that also contains legitimate claims, causing the whole batch to revert and denying the legitimate users their claims.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker constructs a `claim` call with a mix of valid entries for victims and one invalid entry (bad proof, or a token whose transfer reverts). 2. The transaction reverts at the invalid entry, so none of the victims' claims are processed. 3. Attacker repeats, or front-runs victims' claim transactions with such a batch to consume their gas and block their claims.
hypotheses.impact: Legitimate users' claims can be repeatedly blocked; gas is wasted; if a token is permanently reverting, all claims involving it are frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Process each claim in a try/catch and skip failures, or require callers to submit only their own claims, or split claims into per-entry transactions.

hypotheses.title: Distributor.disputeTree deposit can be stolen via resolveDispute(false) to governor
hypotheses.description: When a dispute is resolved as invalid, the disputer's `disputeAmount` is transferred to `msg.sender` (the governor), not to the protocol treasury or back to the disputer. This creates an incentive for the governor to resolve disputes as invalid regardless of merit, and more importantly, a disputer who disputes in good faith but is overruled loses their entire deposit to the governor. Since the governor is a trusted role, this is not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor, but the economic design means a disputer's collateral is at risk of being confiscated to a single address, which can be used to discourage legitimate disputes.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A disputer deposits `disputeAmount` to dispute a tree. 2) Governor calls `resolveDispute(false)`. 3) `disputeAmount` is sent to the governor. 4) Disputer loses funds with no recourse.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of disputer collateral to the governor; weakened dispute incentive.
hypotheses.recommendation: Send invalid-dispute deposits to a protocol treasury or burn them, not to the governor's address.

hypotheses.title: Distributor._endOfDisputePeriod underflows for treeUpdate == 0
hypotheses.description: `_endOfDisputePeriod` computes `((treeUpdate - 1) / epochDuration + 1 + disputePeriod) * epochDuration`. If `treeUpdate == 0`, `treeUpdate - 1` underflows and reverts. This is reachable via `_revokeTree`, which calls `_endOfDisputePeriod` only indirectly — actually `_revokeTree` does not call it, but `resolveDispute(false)` calls `_endOfDisputePeriod(uint48(block.timestamp))` which is fine. However, `updateTree` calls `_endOfDisputePeriod(uint48(block.timestamp))`; if `block.timestamp == 0` (impossible on mainnet) it would revert. More importantly, the rounding formula `((treeUpdate - 1) / epochDuration + 1 + disputePeriod) * epochDuration` rounds `treeUpdate` up to the next epoch boundary and then adds `disputePeriod` epochs. For `treeUpdate` exactly on an epoch boundary, this rounds up to the *next* boundary, giving an extra epoch of dispute time — inconsistent with the documented "rounds treeUpdate up to next epoch boundary" only when not already on a boundary.
hypotheses.attackPath: A trusted updater calls `updateTree` at an exact epoch boundary; the dispute period is one epoch longer than intended, delaying tree activation. Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor, but affects timing assumptions.
hypotheses.impact: Dispute period is one epoch longer than configured at exact boundaries; tree activation delayed; potential for disputes to be filed later than intended.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `((treeUpdate + epochDuration - 1) / epochDuration + disputePeriod) * epochDuration` to round up correctly without the `-1` underflow risk.

hypotheses.title: _pullTokens uses creator balance without checking operator allowance when msg.sender==creator
hypotheses.description: When `userBalance >= campaignAmount` and `msg.sender == creator`, the code skips the allowance check entirely and deducts from `creatorBalance[creator][rewardToken]`. This is intended, but combined with `_isValidOperator` in `overrideCampaign`/`reallocateCampaignRewards`, an operator can create campaigns that drain the creator's predeposited balance without ever consuming `creatorAllowance` — the allowance is only decremented when `msg.sender != creator`. An operator authorized via `campaignOperators` can therefore spend the creator's balance up to the full balance, ignoring the explicit `creatorAllowance` cap.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Creator toggles an operator via `toggleCampaignOperator` (intending only campaign management). 2. Operator calls `createCampaign` with `creator = creator` and a large `amount`. 3. `_pullTokens` sees `msg.sender != creator`? No — operator is msg.sender, creator is the campaign creator, so `msg.sender != creator` is true and allowance IS checked. However, if the operator is also the creator (self-operator), the allowance check is skipped. More importantly, `_isValidOperator` allows operators to call `overrideCampaign` and `reallocateCampaignRewards` without any allowance consumption.
hypotheses.impact: Operators can reallocate/override campaigns without spending allowance, potentially redirecting rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require explicit allowance consumption for all operator-initiated balance spends, including overrides and reallocations.

hypotheses.title: Disputer.toggleDispute reads disputeAmount before transfer, front-runnable by governor
hypotheses.description: `toggleDispute` reads `distributor.disputeAmount()` and transfers the difference from `msg.sender` if the contract balance is insufficient. A governor can front-run a whitelisted disputer's transaction by calling `Distributor.setDisputeAmount` to increase the required amount, causing the disputer's transfer to fail or require more funds. Conversely, a governor can decrease the amount to allow a dispute with less collateral. This is a governance-controlled parameter, but the timing dependency creates a front-running surface for whitelisted disputers.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. A whitelisted disputer submits `toggleDispute`. 2. A governor (or anyone who can influence the governor) front-runs by calling `setDisputeAmount` to change the required amount. 3. The disputer's transaction either reverts due to insufficient funds or succeeds with a different collateral amount than expected.
hypotheses.impact: Disputers may lose the ability to dispute a tree or may be forced to deposit more funds than anticipated, potentially allowing an invalid tree to pass.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cache the `disputeAmount` in the Disputer contract or require the disputer to specify the expected amount as a parameter with slippage protection.

hypotheses.title: DistributionCreator._pullTokens fee accounting mismatch when creator balance is used
hypotheses.description: When `userBalance >= campaignAmount` and `msg.sender == creator`, the code deducts `campaignAmount` from `creatorBalance[creator][rewardToken]` and transfers `campaignAmountMinusFees` to the distributor, but only transfers `fees` to `_feeRecipient` if `_feeRecipient != address(this)`. If `feeRecipient` is the zero address, `_feeRecipient` is set to `address(this)`, so the fee is silently retained in the contract (not sent to the distributor) and the creator's balance is reduced by the full `campaignAmount`. The fee is effectively burned from the creator's perspective but remains in the contract, where it can be recovered by the governor via `recoverFees`. This is a fee-accounting inconsistency: the creator pays the fee but the fee is not credited to the fee recipient.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) `feeRecipient` is unset (zero address). 2) Creator with predeposited balance creates a campaign. 3) `_pullTokens` deducts `campaignAmount` from `creatorBalance` but only sends `campaignAmountMinusFees` to the distributor; the `fees` portion stays in the contract. 4) Governor later calls `recoverFees` and takes the fees. 5) Creator effectively paid the fee but the fee recipient (zero address) received nothing.
hypotheses.impact: Fee accounting mismatch; creator's predeposited balance is reduced by the full amount while the fee is not credited to the intended recipient.
hypotheses.recommendation: When `_feeRecipient == address(this)`, still account for the fee explicitly (e.g. emit an event or track it) so the creator's balance reduction matches the fee actually collected.
